heading: Strict role folders and file names
body: A role type has a domain prefix and a standard suffix. Its file name matches the type name exactly, including case. Rust also accepts the snake_case form of the name, so `money_service.rs` may hold `MoneyService` (ADR 0067). The file sits in the folder with the plural role name, or in a folder nested inside it, such as `services/billing/InvoiceService.ts` (ADR 0091). A nested folder only organizes files: it does not make a new namespace, so two classes with the same name in one realm and language are still an error. Each class in a role folder carries the marker of its role, such as `Service` in `services/`; a class without it fails with `TY1363`, and the message shows the spelling for its language. Examples are MoneyService in services/MoneyService.ts, MoneyStore in stores/MoneyStore.ts and MoneySetup in setups/MoneySetup.ts. Each annotated file holds exactly one class and its imports. Helper types and functions belong in their own files. Each realm has shared role folders, and the two realms use the same folder names. Yon uses server/services, server/stores, server/remotes, server/setups, server/entities, server/helpers and server/converters. Tac uses the same seven under client/. Controllers live in server/controllers, one class in each file. A role file in the wrong folder fails with TY1310. The error names the shared folder where the file belongs. The compiler validates the selected files from the snapshot of the source, which cannot change, and puts them together. Role annotations register validated declarations inside that entry scope. Modifiers such as CacheSettings, Setting and Table add no naming rules. Data types without a role, including the Settings and Checked classes that hold settings and validation rules, live in models/ (ADR 0092). Native Tac keeps its service type first and uses only public client modules. See the Strict annotation layout guide for every supported language.
